cards.title: Whose poster is it?
cards.body:
For a school poster competition, a student types one prompt and gets an amazing poster in seconds. Another student spends a week painting theirs.

Which one is "theirs"? This lesson is about using AI in a way that's fair to you, and to everyone else.

cards.title: Say how you used it
cards.body:
Using AI is often fine. Hiding it usually isn't.

- **Say when and how** you used AI ("I used AI to check my spelling").
- **Follow the rules** of your school, club or competition, and **ask** when you're not sure.
- **Don't claim AI's work as yours**: in a competition, that's not fair on people who did the work.

items.label: "I used AI to check my spelling"
Asking your teacher if AI is allowed
Using AI ideas, writing it, saying so
Entering an AI picture as your own art
Giving an AI-written speech as yours
Saying "no" when asked if you used AI

cards.hint: Look for whether the person is open about the AI's part.
cards.nudge: Using AI isn't the problem. Which ones hide it, or claim its work?
cards.explanation: Saying how you used AI, asking first and writing it yourself are **honest**. Entering AI art as yours, giving an AI speech as yours, or denying it when asked are **not**, however good the result.

cards.title: The people behind it
cards.body:
AI learned from huge amounts of work made by people: artists' pictures, writers' stories, musicians' songs. Many weren't asked, and some are unhappy about it. People disagree about what's fair here, and the rules are still being argued about.

What you can do: **respect people's work**, credit artists you're inspired by, and keep making things in your own way. AI can help, but your ideas and your voice are yours.

cards.prompt: Your teacher says no AI for an essay. You want to use AI just to fix your spelling. What should you do?

options.text: Use a different AI app, so it isn't the one that's banned
options.nudge: The rule is about AI, not one app. What would make it clear?

options.text: Just use it: fixing spelling doesn't really count
options.nudge: It might be fine, but it isn't your call when the rule says no AI. Who decides?

options.text: Ask your teacher whether AI spelling help counts
Use it, and tell your teacher after you hand it in
options.nudge: Saying so is good, but the rule was set before. What should you do first?

cards.hint: When you're not sure if something breaks a rule, who should you ask?
cards.explanation: When you're not sure, **ask first**. Spelling help might be allowed, but it's your teacher's rule to explain, not yours to guess.

cards.title: Fair to everyone
cards.body: Remember bias: a model works better for some people than others when its training data leaves people out. So when AI makes decisions about people, like picking, sorting or scoring them, ask: **who might this be unfair to?** And keep a **person** checking decisions that matter.

cards.prompt: Your class wants to use an AI tool to pick team captains "fairly", based on who talks most in class discussions.

steps.text: What's the best thing to say?

choices.text: "It's fair: everyone is judged by the same rule"
choices.consequence: The same rule for everyone can still be unfair, if the rule itself leaves people out. Quiet kids would never get picked.

choices.text: "Who might this be unfair to? Quieter kids can lead too"
choices.consequence: Exactly. Talking a lot isn't the same as leading well. The class agrees to pick with a person deciding, using more than one thing.

choices.text: "Let it pick, but check it picks the same people every time"
choices.consequence: Picking the same people every time just repeats the unfairness. The question is whether its rule is fair.

cards.hint: Look back at the question to ask whenever AI makes decisions about people.
cards.explanation: Judging by who **talks most** leaves out quieter people who could lead well, even though it's the same rule for everyone. Ask **who it might be unfair to**, and keep a **person** deciding.

cards.prompt: Match each situation to the fair thing to do.

pairs.left: An AI picture for an art contest
pairs.right: Say it's AI, or don't enter it

pairs.left: AI helped you plan an essay
Your art copies an artist's style

cards.hint: Each fix is about being open, or about keeping people in charge.
cards.nudge: One is about credit for someone else's work, one about decisions about people, and two about saying what the AI did.
cards.explanation: Be **open** about AI pictures and essay help, **credit** artists who inspire you, and keep **a person deciding** when AI picks people.

cards.prompt: Your friend's story wins the school writing prize. You know a chatbot wrote most of it.

steps.text: The competition rules said "your own work only". What's the fairest thing to do?

choices.text: Tell everyone in the class what really happened
choices.consequence: That could embarrass your friend in front of everyone before they've had a chance to fix it.

choices.text: Talk to your friend privately, and encourage them to tell the teacher
choices.consequence: Fair to your friend and to the others who entered. If they won't, you can talk to a trusted adult about it.

choices.text: Say nothing: everyone uses AI anyway
choices.consequence: The rules said own work only, and other students did theirs themselves. Staying quiet isn't fair on them.

cards.hint: Think about being fair to the other entrants, and kind to your friend.
cards.explanation: Talking to your friend **privately** gives them the chance to put it right, which is fair to everyone who did their own work. A trusted adult can help if they won't.

cards.title: You know how AI really works
cards.body:
- AI learns **patterns from examples**, so it's only as good, and as fair, as its training data.
- Chatbots pick **likely tokens**, not checked facts: check anything that matters.
- Clear prompts get better answers; say what you want, who it's for and what shape.
- Pictures, voices and videos can be faked: check **outside** the post, and get permission.
- Keep your private stuff private, and use AI **openly and fairly**.

Next: the course final.
